<reason>CON kept the debate anchored to the motion's actual clause—"even if response times increase"—and built a clean comparative: co-response, crisis-trained patrol, and dispatch clinicians deliver de-escalation on the same clock, so the only thing the motion adds is the wait. PRO argued the clinician well but repeatedly slid toward "who comes through the door," which CON correctly labeled as defending the clinician rather than the wait. PRO's honest pressure-round answers became liabilities: routing "suicidal talk without a weapon" to the slow team and admitting there is "no honest minute number" gave CON an uncapped, concrete cost landing on exactly the calls where minutes matter. PRO's best live route—the parent who never calls because of the badge—is plausible and PRO's closing weighing ("the wait smaller than the silence") was sharp, but CON's "who is real" comparison (the caller already on the line vs. a forecast) was the more persuasive weighing. CON's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a minor execution cost and PRO engaged directly enough to keep it competitive rather than lopsided.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 exploitation of [B4.1]: PRO's own dispatch rule sends the slower civilian team to "suicidal talk without a weapon," which CON showed is precisely the unsorted, locked-bathroom-door call where delay is most lethal—turning PRO's concrete answer into evidence that the motion's cost lands on the highest-risk callers with no ceiling.</best_rebuttal>
